Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed with Rokanuddin Mahmud and MK Rahman, Advocates ------ For the Petitioner. 
KS Nabi with Sk Md Serajul Islam, KR Nabi and Shahed Ali Jinnah, Advocates ------For the Respondent No.5
parties:
Anwar Hossain  ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Election Commission of Bangladesh and others  ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
Md Joynul Abedin J: This Rule Nisi under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh was issued calling upon respondents to show cause why the notice being No. Election Commission/Law/Sangsad/Dispute/20/(1)/96 (Part-1)/20 dated 29-3-2000 purporting to ask the petitioner to submit his written statement under section 4 of the Members of Parliament (Determination of Dispute) Act, 1980, Annexure-A, and Reference dated 28-3-2000 by the Speaker to the Election. Commission by Memo No 8(1)12000-Law-2 (Miscellaneous) dated 28-3-2000, Annexure- B, shall not be declared to have been made without any lawful authority and of no legal effect and why the respondents shall not be directed to revoke, cancel, rescind and/or withdraw the same. 

 (ii) respondent No. 2, the Speaker, being convinced that the allegations made by Hossain Mohammad Ershad in his letter dated 24-2-2000 calling upon him to declare the seat of the petitioner vacant by publishing a gazette notification to that effect did not attract the mischief under Article 70(1) of the Constitution causing the seat of the petitioner in the Parliament to be vacant acted illegally and without jurisdiction in referring the matter to the Election Commission treating the same as a dispute under Article 66(4) of the Constitution. 

 8. Mr KS Nabi, the learned Counsel for the respondent No. 5, in reply submits that the Speaker is authorised in law to decide whether the letter dated 24-2-2000 of Hossain Mohammed Ershad making complaint to him raised any dispute regarding the seat of the petitioner being vacant under Article 70(1) and hence the reference of the same as a dispute by the Speaker could not be considered as an illegality. Mr Nabi further submits that since Jatiya Party was no longer a party to the consensus government of the Awami League on the date of complaint on 24-2-2000, his complaint vide letter dated 24-2-2000 did attract the mischief of Article 70(1) of the Constitution and the Speaker was competent to refer it as a dispute to the Election Commission. The Speaker had therefore committed no illegality in referring the matter under section 3 of the Members of Parliament (Determination of Dispute) Act, 1980 to the Election Commission vide Annexure-B. Mr Nabi in this connection referred to and relied on. the decision in the case of Mr Khandker Delwar Hossain, reported in 19 BLD (AD) 276. Mr Nabi also submits that the contention of coram non judice, in the context of the facts of the present case, is totally misdirected and misconceived and, as such, the Election Commission acted in accordance with law in calling for the statements from the petitioner by the impugned Annexure-A. Hence, the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 13. In the judgment of the case of Hossain Mohammad Ershad vs Abdul Muqtadir Chowdhury and another in writ Petition No. 4569 of 2000 (53 DLR 569), to which I am a party, it is held that a mere decision that the member concerned vacated the seat in the parliament on account of his conviction in a criminal offence involving moral turpitude will not ipso facto raise any dispute referable to the Election Commission under Article 66(4) of the Constitution unless the member concerned or any interested party disputed such decision. This view finds support in the case of Secretary, Parliament Secretariate vs Khandker Delwar Hossain, 1999 BLD (AD) 276 = 4 BLC (AD) 273. Reliance of Mr Nabi on the aforesaid case of Khandker Delwar Hossain is therefore misplaced. 

 14. In the present case the Speaker while performing his administrative functions was required to take a decision either way on the basis of the complaint of Hossain Mohammad Ershad in his letter dated 24-2-2000 and he, in fact, took the decision that the petitioner did not vacate his seat. Conversely, if the Speaker took the decision that the petitioner vacated his seat, he was required to inform this fact to the House as required of him under rule 178(3) of the Rules of Procedure of Parliament. If the Parliament was not in session, he was to do it during the inter-session period. In the present case, although the Speaker was convinced that the petitioner having joined the cabinet of the consensus government of Awami League on 23-6-1996 did not resign from his Jatiya Party, he referred the matter to the Election Commission as a dispute for determination despite the fact that no dispute was raised by anyone. Hence, such reference of the dispute as contained in Annexure-B is violative of Article 66(4) of the Constitution and section 3 of the Members of Parliament (Determination of Dispute) Act, 1980 (Act-1 of 1981). 

 15. It appears from Annexure-A that the Election Commission by letter dated 29-3-2000 asked the petitioner to submit his statements accepting the reference made by the Speaker as a dispute without indicating that this decision was taken by the Election Commission and not by its Deputy Secretary (Law) who, in fact, signed Annexure-A of his own in his personal capacity. Since this letter, Annexure-A, does not indicate that this statement was asked for by the Election Commission, which alone had the power to do so, it could not be sustained in law. Such act of asking for the statement by the Deputy Secretary (Law) was coram non judice. Similarly, as it is contended by the petitioner and which is not controverted/denied by "respondent No.5, Hossain Mohammad Ershad, that the proceedings taken by the election Commission on 29-3-2000 was coram non judice inasmuch as such decision could not be said to have been taken by the Election Commission on that date as on that date the Chief Election Commissioner was away from the country. In this case Election Commission has been impleaded as respondent No. 1, but it did not appear and contest-the Rule. In any view of the matter, since there is no material on record or even any assertion by any of the respondents that delegation of power was made by the Chief Election Commissioner either in favour of the said Deputy Secretary (Law) or the other two Election Commissioners, we have no hesitation to hold in acceptance of the contentions made by the learned Counsels for the petitioner that the proceeding taken by the Election Commission vide Annexure-A to the writ petition suffers from coram non judice. This view finds support from the decision in the case of Jatiya Party vs The Election Commission of Bangladesh and others reported in 53 DLR (AD) 38. 

 18. In the instant case when the Election Commission found from the statement of the Speaker dated 28-3-2000 that the Speaker himself was convinced that the allegations contained in the letter dated 24-2-2000 of Hossain Mohammad Ershad did not constitute any circumstance falling under Article 70(1) of the Constitution, the Election Commission was not required to ask for the statements from the petitioner, rather it was required in law to refer the matter back to the Speaker.
